poems:
The bell rings in a building you left twenty years ago.
Someone's kid is running for the door you used.

Crossing guard, orange vest,
one gloved hand up.
The minivan waits like it has been told.
3:02. The meeting could have ended at 2:40, and everyone knows the exact minute.
Peanut butter on a butter knife, unclaimed.
Snack, defined: whatever is reachable without a chair.
The copier warms up like something asked to do a favor.

At 3:06 the bus driver counts heads twice,
gets different numbers,
counts again.

Half a granola bar in a coat pocket, folded shut for later.
Later is now.
A basketball hits a garage door four times, then eight times, then not again all afternoon.

Overheard in the hallway:
'He's fine. He just doesn't like Wednesdays.'
3:10 is when the day decides what it was, and nobody consults you.

3:11. The school bus stops, blinks,
and unloads three arguments into three houses.

Two retirees at a picnic table,
one deck of cards,
no hurry visible from here.

Back of an envelope:
milk
bread
the thing for the sink
something for the lunches

3:14. The water cooler glugs once,
agreeing with nobody in particular.
Quarter past. The whistle goes and forty sneakers agree to stop.

3:16. In the hospital lot, a window down,
a phone call that starts with I'm still here.

3:17 p.m.
Nothing is scheduled.
Something is still due.
The dog has been staring at the driveway for eleven minutes and will not be talked out of it.

PLEASE DO NOT MOVE THE CONES,
say the cones, moved.

3:20. The minivan door slides itself shut,
the day's best engineering.
The floor buffer goes down the hall and back, down the hall and back.

Instructions for the last two hours:
look busy,
be busy,
decide which.

3:23. Chalk on the driveway,
a hopscotch abandoned at seven.

3:24. The apple was a good idea at 3:24.
By 3:31 it will be pretzels.

3:25. The box crusher takes a bale
with real enthusiasm.

3:26. A folder comes home
creased in a way that means something sat on it.

In the teachers' lot, four cars.
Two of them will still be there at seven.

Three time zones east, dinnertime.
Here, the long vowel of the afternoon.
A hose running into a bucket that overflowed.
3:30. The workday folds itself in half and does not fit.

The coil turns.
The bag hangs by one corner.
Now it is a negotiation.
Two crows on a soccer goal, conferring.
Bus 14, three riders, none of them talking, all of them going somewhere they have been before.

Sticker under the folding chair: DO NOT STAND ON THIS.
Everyone has.

3:35 and the email you were dreading arrives.
It is four sentences long.
Two of them are fine.
Sidewalk chalk, half a hopscotch.

3:37. The spreadsheet scrolls back up
to check on itself.
A man in a truck eats lunch at 3:38 because that is when the job let him.
Refrigerator open. No plan.

Cheese stick wrapper, milk ring, twist tie, three grapes underfoot:
the archaeology of a snack.
A nurse writes 1500 on a chart and means right now.

3:42. Practice starts at four.
Everyone is pretending the drive takes ten minutes.
The good pen is in the car.

3:44. A yard-sale sign from Saturday,
still up, still promising.

Quarter to four. Somebody sorts the paperclips
by size, allegedly working.

Sneakers untied on the porch steps,
still holding the shape of the feet.

At 3:47 someone four years old finds a new gear.
It engages until nine.
The mower circles in shrinking rectangles.
A lanyard, a badge, a photograph taken in a worse year.
Ten minutes to the hour, and the meeting will use all ten, because it can.

3:51. The case number read back digit by digit,
a duet nobody wanted.
3:52. The afternoon has a soft spot in it and most people fall through around now.

A broom leaned in a corner,
bristles worn to one side.

Kitchen counter:
bananas going,
mail unopened,
a permission slip due tomorrow.
Five to four, and the gym lot fills with people who told themselves this morning they would.
A kid explains the entire plot of something to an adult who is nodding at the wrong parts.

3:57. The to-do list is renamed
a draft.

3:58. A recipe read twice,
trusted once.
Four o'clock is going to happen whether or not the report does.
